title: Postgres Transactions & Locking: A Field Handbook
summary: A dense study-notes series on how Postgres isolates concurrent transactions — MVCC internals, the three usable isolation levels, the anomalies each one still allows, and the locking tools (row locks, deadlock handling, advisory locks) you need to write correct concurrent code.

chapters.title: Transactions & ACID: The Ground Rules
points: A transaction is a unit of work that is all-or-nothing: BEGIN ... COMMIT applies everything, ROLLBACK applies nothing.
ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (constraints hold at commit), Isolation (concurrent txns don't see each other's mess), Durability (committed data survives crash).
Isolation is the only ACID property with a dial — SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL trades concurrency for correctness.
Postgres is autocommit by default: every bare statement runs inside its own implicit transaction.
Multi-statement example: BEGIN; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1; UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal + 100 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;
Any error inside a transaction block poisons it: the session enters 'current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block' until ROLLBACK.
SAVEPOINT sp1; ... ROLLBACK TO sp1; lets you undo part of a transaction without losing the whole thing — this is how psql \set ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK and most ORMs implement nested transactions.

Savepoints are not free: each one consumes a subtransaction XID; thousands per transaction cause the SubtransSLRU contention known as 'subtransaction overflow' (>64 subxacts per txn spills the cache).
SQL standard defines four levels: Read Uncommitted, Read Committed, Repeatable Read, Serializable.
Postgres implements only three distinct behaviors — Read Uncommitted is accepted syntactically but silently behaves as Read Committed; dirty reads are impossible in Postgres.

Standard anomalies: dirty read (see uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same row changes between reads), phantom read (new rows match a re-run query), serialization anomaly (concurrent result matches no serial order).
Postgres matrix: Read Committed allows non-repeatable + phantom + serialization anomalies; Repeatable Read blocks non-repeatable and phantom reads but allows write skew; Serializable blocks all four.
Default level is Read Committed — chosen for throughput, not for correctness of complex business invariants.
Set per transaction: BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ; or for the session: SET SESSION CHARACTERISTICS AS TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE.
The isolation level cannot be changed after the first query of a transaction has executed.
Read-only hint: SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY blocks writes and, combined with DEFERRABLE + SERIALIZABLE, gives a snapshot that never aborts.

chapters.title: MVCC: How Postgres Sees the Past
points: MVCC = Multi-Version Concurrency Control: writers never block readers, readers never block writers, because each row version is kept until no snapshot needs it.
Every heap tuple carries hidden system columns: xmin (XID that inserted it) and xmax (XID that deleted or locked it).
UPDATE is not in-place: it marks the old tuple's xmax and inserts a brand new tuple version with a fresh xmin. DELETE only stamps xmax.
Inspect it directly: SELECT xmin, xmax, ctid, * FROM accounts WHERE id = 1;
ctid is the physical (page, offset) location — it changes on every UPDATE, which is why ctid is unsafe as a durable row identity.
An XID (transaction id) is assigned lazily — read-only transactions get a virtual xid and never burn a real one. Check with SELECT txid_current() vs pg_current_xact_id().
A snapshot is the triple (xmin_horizon, xmax, xip_list): the oldest still-running XID, the next unassigned XID, and the list of in-progress XIDs.
Visibility rule: a tuple is visible if its xmin committed and is in the snapshot, and its xmax is null, aborted, or not yet visible in the snapshot.
Commit status lives in the commit log (pg_xact/CLOG); hint bits are written back onto tuples so later reads skip the CLOG lookup — this is why the first SELECT after a big write can dirty pages.
Dead tuples are reclaimed by VACUUM only once no snapshot can still see them; a single long-running transaction pins the horizon and blocks cleanup database-wide.
Bloat is the direct cost of MVCC: heavy update tables grow because old versions linger. Watch n_dead_tup in pg_stat_user_tables.
HOT (Heap-Only Tuple) updates avoid new index entries when no indexed column changed and the new version fits on the same page — a major reason to avoid indexing hot columns.
XIDs are 32-bit and wrap around; freezing (VACUUM FREEZE) rewrites old xmin as frozen. Ignoring autovacuum eventually forces the database into wraparound-protection shutdown.
Consequence for isolation: the isolation level is essentially just a policy for *when a new snapshot is taken*.
Snapshot export: pg_export_snapshot() + SET TRANSACTION SNAPSHOT lets parallel workers (and pg_dump) read exactly the same consistent view.

chapters.title: Read Committed: The Default and Its Surprises
points: Read Committed takes a NEW snapshot at the start of every individual statement, not at BEGIN.
Result: two identical SELECTs in one transaction can return different data — a non-repeatable read.
It sees only data committed before the statement began; it never sees uncommitted data or changes committed mid-statement.
Demo: session A runs BEGIN; SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id=1; -- 100. Session B updates to 500 and commits. Session A re-runs the same SELECT and gets 500.
Writes behave differently: if an UPDATE hits a row locked by another transaction, it BLOCKS until that transaction ends.
If the blocker commits, Read Committed does an EPQ (EvalPlanQual) re-check: it re-reads the newest row version and re-evaluates the WHERE clause against it.
Consequence of EPQ: the WHERE clause is re-checked but the rest of the statement's snapshot is not — the same statement can see a mix of old and new data.
Classic trap: UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id=1 AND bal >= 100; is safe (predicate re-checked), but UPDATE ... SET bal = 400 based on a value you SELECTed earlier is not.
If the blocker rolled back, the waiter proceeds against the original version as if nothing happened.
If the blocker DELETEd the row, the waiting UPDATE simply skips it — the row silently vanishes from the update's scope.
Read Committed never throws serialization failures, so no retry loop is required — that is its main operational appeal.
It permits phantom reads: a second execution of SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE user_id=7 can return more rows.
It permits lost updates through the read-modify-write pattern in application code.
Good fit for: short OLTP statements, single-row updates expressed as self-referencing SQL (bal = bal - 100), web request handlers.
Bad fit for: multi-statement reports, any invariant spanning more than one row, balance checks split across a SELECT then an UPDATE.

chapters.title: Repeatable Read: One Snapshot for the Whole Transaction
points: Repeatable Read takes ONE snapshot at the first statement of the transaction and reuses it until COMMIT.
Every SELECT in the transaction therefore returns the same rows and same values — reads are stable and consistent.
Postgres's Repeatable Read is stricter than the SQL standard requires: it is true Snapshot Isolation, so phantom reads are also prevented.
That means both non-repeatable reads and phantoms are gone, without any predicate locking cost.
Writes still see the present, not the past: an UPDATE cannot silently overwrite a row modified after the snapshot.
Instead you get: ERROR: could not serialize access due to concurrent update (SQLSTATE 40001) — the transaction aborts entirely.
There is no partial recovery: 40001 poisons the whole transaction, savepoints do not save you, the only fix is ROLLBACK and re-run from scratch.
Any application using Repeatable Read MUST have a retry loop; without one you have converted correctness bugs into user-visible 500s.
First-updater-wins is the rule: the transaction that commits first survives, the other one is told to retry.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside Repeatable Read can also raise 40001 if the target row moved since the snapshot.
Snapshot is taken at the first statement, not at BEGIN — so BEGIN; <sleep 10s>; SELECT ...; still sees fresh data at the SELECT.
Ideal for: reports and exports that must be internally consistent across many queries, backups, batch reads, anything reading the same data twice.
Cost: a long Repeatable Read transaction pins the vacuum horizon and drives bloat — keep them short or accept the storage churn.
It still allows WRITE SKEW: two transactions read overlapping data, write disjoint rows, and together break an invariant neither broke alone.
Write skew is the exact gap Serializable exists to close.

chapters.title: Serializable (SSI): Correct by Construction
points: Serializable guarantees that any set of concurrent transactions produces a result identical to SOME serial execution of them.
Postgres implements it as SSI — Serializable Snapshot Isolation — built on top of Repeatable Read's snapshot, not on two-phase locking.
It is optimistic: transactions never block each other for isolation reasons; conflicts are detected and one victim is aborted at commit or read time.
SSI tracks read dependencies with SIREAD predicate locks — non-blocking marks that record 'this transaction read this data'.
Predicate locks have granularity: tuple, page, or relation. Under memory pressure they escalate upward, causing more false-positive aborts.
Tuning knobs: max_pred_locks_per_transaction, max_pred_locks_per_relation, max_pred_locks_per_page.
Detection targets the 'dangerous structure': two rw-antidependencies in a row, where a pivot transaction is both read-by and reads-from concurrent transactions.
Failure mode: ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies among transactions — again SQLSTATE 40001, again the only cure is retry.
The error hint is explicit: 'The transaction might succeed if retried' — retries usually succeed because contention has cleared.
Crucial rule: ALL participating transactions must run Serializable. One Read Committed writer sneaking in breaks the guarantee entirely.
SERIALIZABLE READ ONLY DEFERRABLE waits until it can take a snapshot guaranteed never to abort — perfect for long consistent reports with zero retry risk.
SSI cost: extra memory for predicate locks, some CPU for conflict tracking, and a false-positive abort rate that rises with contention.
It cannot protect side effects outside the database — a retried transaction re-sends the email you already sent. Keep external effects out of retryable transactions.
Best fit: complex invariants that no single row can enforce (scheduling, double-booking, on-call rotation, inventory across rows).
Rule of thumb: Serializable is cheaper than the concurrency bugs it prevents when writes are low-contention; measure the 40001 rate before rejecting it.

chapters.title: Lost Updates & Write Skew: The Anomalies That Bite
points: Lost update: two transactions read the same value, both compute a new one from it, both write — the second silently erases the first.
The bug pattern is read-modify-write in application code: SELECT bal INTO x; x = x - 100; UPDATE SET bal = x;
Under Read Committed the second UPDATE overwrites cleanly and nobody is told. Concurrency bug, no error.
Fix 1 — atomic SQL: UPDATE accounts SET bal = bal - 100 WHERE id = 1 AND bal >= 100; the value is computed by the database from the current row.
Fix 2 — pessimistic lock: SELECT bal FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE; forces other writers to wait until you commit.
Fix 3 — optimistic lock: add a version column and use UPDATE ... SET v = v+1 WHERE id = 1 AND v = 7; check the affected row count and retry on 0.
Fix 4 — raise isolation: Repeatable Read turns the lost update into a 40001 error you can retry, converting silence into a signal.
Always check affected-row counts on conditional updates — a 0-row UPDATE is a failed business operation, not a no-op.
Write skew: two transactions read an overlapping set, each writes a DIFFERENT row, and the combination breaks a constraint neither violated alone.
Canonical example — on-call: both doctors query 'count of on-call doctors >= 2', both see 2, each sets themselves off-call, hospital ends with zero.
Write skew survives Repeatable Read because the two transactions never update the same row — first-updater-wins never fires.
Only Serializable (or an explicit lock on a shared row / a materialized conflict row) prevents write skew.
Phantom-driven write skew: 'insert a meeting if no overlapping meeting exists' — both transactions see an empty result set, both insert.
Materializing the conflict is the classic workaround: create a row per resource (per room, per day) and lock it FOR UPDATE so the phantom becomes a real row conflict.
Constraint-first alternative: an EXCLUDE constraint with tsrange && makes double-booking impossible at any isolation level — prefer DB constraints over transaction ceremony.
Decision rule: single-row invariant → atomic UPDATE; cross-row invariant → Serializable or a materialized lock row; uniqueness/overlap → a real constraint.

chapters.title: Explicit Locks: Rows, Tables, and When to Reach for Them
points: MVCC handles reads; explicit locks handle the cases where you must serialize writers by hand.
Row-level lock modes, weakest to strongest: FOR KEY SHARE, FOR SHARE, FOR NO KEY UPDATE, FOR UPDATE.
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE blocks other FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, UPDATE and DELETE on those rows — but never blocks plain SELECTs.
SELECT ... FOR SHARE allows other readers to also take FOR SHARE but blocks writers — useful for 'this row must not change while I reference it'.
FOR NO KEY UPDATE is what a normal UPDATE takes when no key column changes; it is weaker so it does not block foreign-key checks.
FOR KEY SHARE is what a foreign-key check takes on the parent row — this is why child inserts no longer block parent updates in modern Postgres.
Row locks live in the tuple's xmax and in multixact structures; they are held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK and are never released early.
NOWAIT: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT raises 'could not obtain lock on row' immediately instead of queuing — good for interactive UIs.
SKIP LOCKED: skips rows another transaction holds — the standard way to build a work queue.
Queue pattern: UPDATE jobs SET state='running' WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM jobs WHERE state='queued' ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 1) RETURNING *;

Table-level lock modes matter too: ACCESS SHARE (SELECT), ROW EXCLUSIVE (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE), SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE (VACUUM, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY), ACCESS EXCLUSIVE (ALTER TABLE, DROP, TRUNCATE).
ACCESS EXCLUSIVE conflicts with everything — a migration that waits on this lock queues every subsequent query behind it and takes the site down.
Migration safety: always SET lock_timeout = '2s' before DDL so a blocked ALTER fails fast instead of forming a queue.
Diagnose with pg_locks joined to pg_stat_activity; pg_blocking_pids(pid) gives the blocking chain directly.
Guardrails: lock_timeout caps waiting for a lock, statement_timeout caps total statement runtime, idle_in_transaction_session_timeout kills the abandoned transaction holding everything hostage.

chapters.title: Deadlocks: Detection, Cause, and Cure
points: Deadlock = a cycle of waits: A holds row 1 and wants row 2, B holds row 2 and wants row 1. Neither can proceed.
Postgres does not prevent deadlocks; it detects them and kills one transaction as the victim.
The error: ERROR: deadlock detected / DETAIL: Process 123 waits for ShareLock on transaction 456; blocked by process 789. SQLSTATE 40P01.
Detection is lazy: a waiter only runs the cycle-detection algorithm after waiting deadlock_timeout (default 1s), because checking is expensive.
Tuning: lowering deadlock_timeout detects faster but burns CPU on every lock wait; raising it hides deadlocks behind latency.
log_lock_waits = on logs any wait exceeding deadlock_timeout — the cheapest way to find contention before it becomes a deadlock.
The victim is chosen by the detector, not by age or priority — your code cannot assume which side dies.
Cause 1 — inconsistent lock ordering: one code path updates accounts in id order, another in reverse order.
Fix: enforce a global ordering. UPDATE ... WHERE id IN (1,2) ORDER BY id, or always lock the lower id first.
Cause 2 — lock upgrade: SELECT (share) then UPDATE (exclusive) on the same row from two sessions. Fix: take FOR UPDATE on the first read.
Cause 3 — foreign keys: concurrent inserts into a child table touching the same parent, or unique-index insert conflicts where each waits on the other's uncommitted row.
Cause 4 — multi-row statements with nondeterministic order: a bulk UPDATE without ORDER BY can visit rows in different physical orders in different sessions.
Deadlock is retryable: 40P01, like 40001, means 'roll back the whole transaction and run it again'. Retry with jitter to avoid re-colliding.
Reduce the window: keep transactions short, acquire all locks up front, never hold a lock across an HTTP call or user think-time.
Diagnosis workflow: read the DETAIL line for both PIDs, find both statements in the log, compare their lock acquisition order, then impose an ordering.

chapters.title: Advisory Locks: Application Locks, Database-Enforced
points: Advisory locks are locks on arbitrary 64-bit numbers you invent — Postgres enforces mutual exclusion but attaches no meaning to the key.
Use them when the thing you must serialize is not a row: a cron job, a migration runner, an external API call, a leader election.
Two key shapes: one bigint (pg_advisory_lock(bigint)) or two ints (pg_advisory_lock(int, int)) — the two-int form is a convenient namespace + id.
Session-scoped: pg_advisory_lock(key) holds until pg_advisory_unlock(key) or the session disconnects. Survives COMMIT and ROLLBACK.
Transaction-scoped: pg_advisory_xact_lock(key) is released automatically at end of transaction and CANNOT be unlocked manually — safer by default.
Non-blocking variants return boolean instead of waiting: SELECT pg_try_advisory_lock(42); returns false if someone else holds it.
Singleton-worker pattern: IF NOT pg_try_advisory_lock(hashtext('nightly-report')) THEN exit; — guarantees exactly one instance across all app servers.
Shared variants exist too: pg_advisory_lock_shared / pg_advisory_xact_lock_shared for many-readers-one-writer coordination.
Session locks are re-entrant: locking twice in the same session requires two unlocks. This is a common leak source.
Generate stable keys from strings with hashtext('my-job') or ('x'||md5(name))::bit(64)::bigint — but beware collisions across unrelated features; namespace with the two-int form.
Connection poolers are the classic footgun: with PgBouncer in transaction pooling mode, session-level advisory locks leak onto whichever backend served you. Use pg_advisory_xact_lock there.
Advisory locks participate in the same deadlock detector as regular locks — you can deadlock an advisory lock against a row lock.
Inspect with SELECT * FROM pg_locks WHERE locktype = 'advisory'; the classid/objid columns hold your key halves.
Advisory locks do not prevent data anomalies — they only prevent concurrent execution of code paths that agree to ask for the lock.
Compare to alternatives: FOR UPDATE on a real row is better when a row exists; advisory locks win when the resource is abstract or spans tables.

chapters.title: Playbook: Choosing, Retrying, and Monitoring
points: Decision tree: single-row invariant → Read Committed + atomic UPDATE. Consistent multi-query read → Repeatable Read. Cross-row invariant → Serializable. Non-row resource → advisory lock.
Never default to Serializable everywhere out of fear; never default to Read Committed everywhere out of habit. Choose per transaction.
Retry contract: catch SQLSTATE 40001 (serialization failure) and 40P01 (deadlock) — both mean roll back and re-run the whole transaction unchanged.
Never retry 23505 (unique violation) or 23503 (FK violation) as if they were transient; those are logic errors.
Retry loop shape: up to ~5 attempts, exponential backoff with jitter, full ROLLBACK before each retry, and a metric counting retries per endpoint.
Side effects must be idempotent or moved outside the transaction — the retried body runs again from the top.
Keep transactions short: open late, commit early, and never hold one open across network I/O or user input.
Set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout so a forgotten BEGIN cannot pin the vacuum horizon forever.
Monitor: pg_stat_database.xact_commit vs xact_rollback for abort rate, deadlocks column for deadlock count, pg_stat_activity for wait_event_type = 'Lock'.
Find long transactions: SELECT pid, now()-xact_start AS age, state, query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE xact_start IS NOT NULL ORDER BY age DESC;
Find blockers: SELECT pid, pg_blocking_pids(pid), query FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0;
Watch bloat as the tax on all of this: n_dead_tup in pg_stat_user_tables and the age(datfrozenxid) wraparound margin.
Prefer database constraints (UNIQUE, CHECK, EXCLUDE, foreign keys) over transaction-level tricks — a constraint holds regardless of isolation level or application bug.
Test concurrency for real: Postgres's own isolation tester (src/test/isolation, .spec files) and pgbench custom scripts reproduce races that unit tests never will.

Summary table to memorize — Read Committed: per-statement snapshot, no retries, allows lost update + write skew. Repeatable Read: per-transaction snapshot, retries on concurrent update, allows write skew. Serializable: per-transaction snapshot + SSI, retries on dependency cycles, allows nothing.
Final rule: correctness is chosen deliberately. Pick the weakest isolation level that still makes the invariant impossible to break, then prove it with a concurrent test.
